# The statistical mechanics of conditional wavefunctions {#sec-projected-ensembles}

Ordinary thermalization answers a question about averages: what will a local observer measure after a closed many-body system evolves for a long time? A more detailed question becomes possible if that observer also receives a measurement record from the rest of the system. Conditioned on the record, the observer assigns a different local wavefunction on every run. What statistical law describes these wavefunctions?

This chapter develops the tools needed to make that question precise. The central distinction is between a mixed density operator and an ensemble of pure states realizing it. We will derive a hierarchy of tests of ensemble randomness, identify what each test measures, and explain why equilibration of a density operator leaves substantial physics unresolved. The examples and calculations below are elementary constructions; their purpose is to expose the mathematical structure underlying the research literature.

## Measuring a bath produces an ensemble

Let a finite quantum system have Hilbert space $\mathcal H_A\otimes\mathcal H_B$, with dimensions $d_A$ and $d_B$. The letters $A$ and $B$ designate the retained subsystem and the measured environment. Calling $B$ a bath does not assume that it is an external thermostat: the complete state can be pure and its dynamics unitary.

Expand that state in a chosen orthonormal basis of $B$:

$$
\lvert\Psi\rangle_{AB}
=\sum_{a=1}^{d_A}\sum_{z=1}^{d_B}\Psi_{az}
\lvert a\rangle_A\lvert z\rangle_B
=\sum_z\lvert\widetilde\psi_z\rangle_A\lvert z\rangle_B.
$$ {#eq-pe-expansion}

The tilde indicates that a vector is not normalized. A projective measurement of $B$ gives outcome $z$ with probability

$$
p_z=\langle\widetilde\psi_z\vert\widetilde\psi_z\rangle,
\qquad
\lvert\psi_z\rangle=\frac{\lvert\widetilde\psi_z\rangle}{\sqrt{p_z}}.
$$ {#eq-pe-born}

Outcomes with $p_z=0$ can be omitted. The **projected ensemble** is the probability distribution

$$
\mathcal E_{\Psi,B}=\{p_z,\lvert\psi_z\rangle\}_z.
$$ {#eq-pe-definition}

The Born weights are essential. Giving every nonzero outcome equal weight generally defines a different distribution and need not reproduce any physical reduced state.

Indeed, averaging the projectors in @eq-pe-born gives

$$
\sum_zp_z\lvert\psi_z\rangle\langle\psi_z\rvert
=\sum_z\lvert\widetilde\psi_z\rangle\langle\widetilde\psi_z\rvert
=\operatorname{Tr}_B\lvert\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi\rvert
\equiv\rho_A.
$$ {#eq-pe-average}

The cancellation of normalization factors makes this identity exact. It also explains why ordinary local measurements see only $\rho_A$ when the bath record is discarded.

There are two distinct sources of probability here. Quantum measurement generates $z$ with Born probability even when $\lvert\Psi\rangle$ is fixed. Separately, a theorist may sample $\lvert\Psi\rangle$ from a distribution, for example an ensemble of random circuits. Averaging over the latter is a mathematical or preparation average. A statement about the projected ensemble of a typical single state is stronger than a statement only about its average over preparations.

### Worked example: a Bell pair has many local ensembles

Consider

$$
\lvert\Phi^+\rangle
=\frac{\lvert00\rangle+\lvert11\rangle}{\sqrt2}.
$$ {#eq-pe-bell}

Measuring the second qubit in the $Z$ basis prepares $\lvert0\rangle$ or $\lvert1\rangle$ on the first, each with probability $1/2$. Measuring it in the $X$ basis prepares $\lvert+\rangle$ or $\lvert-\rangle$, where $\lvert\pm\rangle=(\lvert0\rangle\pm\lvert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$. Both ensembles average to $I/2$. Nevertheless, their conditional $Z$ expectation values have different fluctuations:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_{\mathcal E_Z}\langle Z\rangle_\psi^2&=1,\\
\mathbb E_{\mathcal E_X}\langle Z\rangle_\psi^2&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-pe-bell-variance}

This is already a measurable difference between ensembles that share a density operator. It requires knowing which bath outcome occurred and estimating the local expectation value for that conditional state. It cannot be inferred from a single unconditioned local measurement.

The freedom to obtain different ensembles by measuring a purification is general. The Hughston–Jozsa–Wootters classification describes all pure-state decompositions of a fixed density operator and their realization by suitable measurements on an auxiliary system [@hjw1993]. Fixed local projective measurements constitute a physically important restricted choice within this broader freedom.

## Moments turn distributions into quantum states

A probability distribution over pure states can be characterized by averages of products of amplitudes and their complex conjugates. The convenient quantum object collecting these averages is

$$
M_{\mathcal E}^{(k)}
=\sum_zp_z
\bigl(\lvert\psi_z\rangle\langle\psi_z\rvert\bigr)^{\otimes k},
\qquad k=1,2,\ldots .
$$ {#eq-pe-moments}

It is a positive, unit-trace operator acting on $k$ copies of $\mathcal H_A$. It is not generally equal to $\rho_A^{\otimes k}$. In the latter object each copy is drawn independently, whereas @eq-pe-moments uses the *same conditional state* on all copies before averaging its label.

For observables $O_1,\ldots,O_k$,

$$
\mathbb E_{\mathcal E}
\prod_{j=1}^k\langle O_j\rangle_\psi
=\operatorname{Tr}\left[
(O_1\otimes\cdots\otimes O_k)M_{\mathcal E}^{(k)}
\right].
$$ {#eq-pe-nonlinear-observable}

Thus the first moment gives mean expectation values, the second gives variances and covariances, and higher moments resolve more detailed fluctuations. A thermal density operator fixes the first of these and leaves the others undetermined.

Taking a partial trace over any copy of $M^{(k)}$ gives $M^{(k-1)}$, because a normalized pure-state projector has trace one. Consequently, matching a higher moment automatically matches every lower moment.

For two target ensembles define

$$
\Delta_k(\mathcal E,\mathcal F)
=\frac12\left\|M_{\mathcal E}^{(k)}
-M_{\mathcal F}^{(k)}\right\|_1,
\qquad
\|X\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{X^\dagger X}.
$$ {#eq-pe-distance}

This trace distance has an operational meaning. Suppose an experimenter receives $k$ identical copies of a state whose unknown label was drawn from either ensemble. The best collective measurement distinguishes the two possibilities with success probability $(1+\Delta_k)/2$, for equal prior probabilities. The statement concerns indistinguishability of these *averaged $k$-copy experiments*; it does not say that the two probability measures are close in every conceivable metric.

Partial trace cannot increase trace distance, so $\Delta_{k-1}\leq\Delta_k$. A second-moment discrepancy cannot hide behind a matching third moment.

## What does uniform randomness mean?

The **Haar ensemble** of pure states is the distribution invariant under every unitary transformation on a $d$-dimensional Hilbert space. One construction is to sample $d$ independent standard complex Gaussian variables $g_a$ and normalize their vector:

$$
\lvert\phi\rangle=\frac{\sum_ag_a\lvert a\rangle}
{\sqrt{\sum_a|g_a|^2}}.
$$ {#eq-pe-gaussian-haar}

The complex Gaussian density depends only on $\sum_a|g_a|^2$ and is unchanged by unitary rotations. Its direction is therefore uniform. This construction makes clear that Haar randomness concerns the direction of a state vector, with overall phase physically irrelevant.

We can derive its moment operator without integrating individual amplitudes. Every vector $\lvert\phi\rangle^{\otimes k}$ lies in the fully symmetric subspace of $\mathcal H^{\otimes k}$, since exchanging any two copies leaves it unchanged. Haar invariance also makes its averaged projector commute with $U^{\otimes k}$ for every unitary $U$. The action on the symmetric subspace is irreducible, so this average is proportional to its identity operator, the symmetric projector $P_{\mathrm{sym}}^{(k)}$. Unit trace fixes the constant:

$$
M_{\mathrm H}^{(k)}
=\frac{P_{\mathrm{sym}}^{(k)}}{D_k},
\qquad
D_k=\binom{d+k-1}{k},
\qquad
P_{\mathrm{sym}}^{(k)}
=\frac1{k!}\sum_{\pi\in S_k}U_\pi.
$$ {#eq-pe-haar-moments}

Here $S_k$ is the permutation group and $U_\pi$ permutes tensor factors. The dimension formula counts occupations of $k$ indistinguishable objects among $d$ basis states: nonnegative integers $n_1+\cdots+n_d=k$.

For $k=2$, the only permutations are the identity and the swap $F$, with $F\lvert a,b\rangle=\lvert b,a\rangle$. Therefore

$$
M_{\mathrm H}^{(2)}
=\frac{I+F}{d(d+1)}.
$$ {#eq-pe-haar-second}

Using $\operatorname{Tr}[(O\otimes P)F]=\operatorname{Tr}(OP)$ yields

$$
\mathbb E_{\mathrm H}\langle O\rangle_\phi\langle P\rangle_\phi
=\frac{\operatorname{Tr}O\,\operatorname{Tr}P+
\operatorname{Tr}(OP)}{d(d+1)}.
$$ {#eq-pe-haar-covariance}

For traceless Hermitian $O$, its conditional expectation has variance $\operatorname{Tr}(O^2)/[d(d+1)]$. In particular, a Haar-random qubit has $\mathbb E\langle Z\rangle^2=1/3$, between the two values in @eq-pe-bell-variance. Randomness is therefore quantitatively different from either ensemble of orthogonal antipodal states.

### Worked example: the Bloch sphere and a finite design

A pure qubit projector is

$$
\rho_{\boldsymbol n}=\frac{I+\boldsymbol n\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma}{2},
\qquad |\boldsymbol n|=1.
$$ {#eq-pe-bloch}

Its first moment depends on $\mathbb E n_i$; its second also depends on $\mathbb E n_in_j$. Uniform spherical measure obeys $\mathbb E n_i=0$ and $\mathbb E n_in_j=\delta_{ij}/3$. These follow from rotational invariance and $\sum_i n_i^2=1$.

Now choose the four unit vectors

$$
\frac{(1,1,1)}{\sqrt3},\quad
\frac{(1,-1,-1)}{\sqrt3},\quad
\frac{(-1,1,-1)}{\sqrt3},\quad
\frac{(-1,-1,1)}{\sqrt3}
$$ {#eq-pe-tetrahedron}

with equal probabilities. Their mean vanishes, each diagonal second moment is $1/3$, and each off-diagonal second moment cancels. Their ensemble therefore reproduces the Haar first and second moments exactly, although it contains only four states.

Such an ensemble is a **state $2$-design**. More generally a state $k$-design satisfies $M_{\mathcal E}^{(k)}=M_{\mathrm H}^{(k)}$. A finite design need not resemble a continuous cloud visually; it reproduces a specified set of experiments. The tetrahedral ensemble is not a $3$-design: its average $n_xn_yn_z$ equals $1/(3\sqrt3)$, whereas the spherical average vanishes.

## Frame potentials and finite-environment limitations

A useful scalar diagnostic is the frame potential

$$
\mathcal F_k(\mathcal E)
=\sum_{z,z'}p_zp_{z'}|\langle\psi_z\vert\psi_{z'}\rangle|^{2k}
=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[(M_{\mathcal E}^{(k)})^2\bigr].
$$ {#eq-pe-frame-potential}

To establish the second equality, multiply two rank-one tensor projectors and take their trace. Each copy contributes $|\langle\psi_z\vert\psi_{z'}\rangle|^2$.

Because $M_{\mathcal E}^{(k)}$ lives in a space of dimension $D_k$, its purity is at least $1/D_k$. Equality holds only for $P_{\mathrm{sym}}^{(k)}/D_k$, so

$$
\mathcal F_k\geq\frac1{D_k},
\qquad
\left\|M_{\mathcal E}^{(k)}-M_{\mathrm H}^{(k)}\right\|_2^2
=\mathcal F_k-\frac1{D_k}.
$$ {#eq-pe-frame-excess}

In this equation $\|X\|_2=\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}(X^\dagger X)}$. The last identity follows by expanding the square and using $\operatorname{Tr}(M_{\mathcal E}^{(k)}P_{\mathrm{sym}}^{(k)})=1$. Frame-potential excess is exactly a squared Hilbert–Schmidt distance. Turning it into trace distance can introduce a dimension factor through $\|X\|_1\leq\sqrt{D_k}\|X\|_2$; small unnormalized frame-potential excess alone can therefore be misleading as $d$ or $k$ grows.

There is also a simple obstruction to exact designs at finite bath size. A rank-one projective measurement has at most $d_B$ outcomes, so $M_{\mathcal E}^{(k)}$ has rank at most $d_B$. Let its support have dimension $r\leq d_B$. The target Haar moment puts probability $(D_k-r)/D_k$ outside that support, while the actual moment puts probability zero there. Measuring the projector onto the complement gives

$$
\Delta_k(\mathcal E,\mathrm H)
\geq 1-\frac{r}{D_k}
\geq 1-\frac{d_B}{D_k}
\quad\text{if }d_B<D_k.
$$ {#eq-pe-rank-bound}

Thus a finite bath cannot produce an exact design of arbitrarily high order on a nontrivial subsystem. Claims of simultaneous equality of every moment in dynamical models must specify a thermodynamic limit. For a fixed order $k$, an adequately large finite bath can approximate the required statistics.

## Why random many-body states give Haar-like projected ensembles

The Gaussian construction offers an intuitive derivation. Generate a random global state by a $d_A\times d_B$ matrix $G$ of independent complex Gaussian entries and normalize all entries together. Its $z$th column can be written $G_z=r_z\phi_z$, where $\phi_z$ is a Haar direction on $A$ and $r_z\geq0$ is its length.

Gaussian rotational invariance makes $\phi_z$ independent of $r_z$. The projected ensemble is

$$
p_z=\frac{r_z^2}{\sum_{z'}r_{z'}^2},
\qquad \lvert\psi_z\rangle=\lvert\phi_z\rangle.
$$ {#eq-pe-random-columns}

Since the weight depends only on radii, it introduces no preferred direction. Averaging over global preparations therefore gives $\mathbb E_\Psi M_{\mathcal E_\Psi}^{(k)}=M_{\mathrm H}^{(k)}$ exactly for every finite $k$.

That identity alone does not prove that one global state supplies an approximate design. For that stronger conclusion, fix $d_A,k$ and increase $d_B$. The numerator of the weighted average in @eq-pe-random-columns is a sum of independent random matrices, while its denominator is a sum of independent positive random variables. Their relative fluctuations become small. Entrywise laws of large numbers suffice in this fixed finite-dimensional moment space to give convergence of the single-state moment to its Haar value. Quantitative high-probability statements require bounds controlling dimension, desired error, and design order together.

This calculation distinguishes entanglement from sufficient complexity. A maximally entangled state with $d_A=d_B$ has a maximally mixed $\rho_A$, yet a fixed orthonormal measurement produces only $d_A$ orthogonal states. Its second moment cannot be Haar by @eq-pe-rank-bound. Large entanglement supplies many possible local states; scrambling arranges their probabilities and directions appropriately.

The physical question is whether local dynamics can generate the statistics suggested by this random-state benchmark, and how rapidly. The ensemble is physically obtained by measuring one evolved many-body state. It need not require choosing a new random global unitary for every member of the ensemble.

## Exact dynamical results and the hierarchy of design times

Ho and Choi proved finite-time emergence of exact projected state designs in a special chaotic kicked Ising setting, after taking an infinite-bath limit [@HoChoi2022]. These results are existence theorems for specified dynamics, initial states, measurement bases, and limits. They establish that a locally thermal reduced state can be accompanied by much stronger universal statistics; they do not establish identical finite-time behavior for arbitrary chaotic Hamiltonians.

The structural idea is **space–time duality**. A circuit amplitude is a tensor network with a physical time direction and a spatial direction. Fixing the final bath outcomes turns the contraction along space into a sequence of effective maps on degrees of freedom associated with the time boundary. A map that is unitary in the original time direction need not be unitary after this rotation. In special circuits it is unitary in both directions, a property called dual unitarity. Compatible boundary states and measurement bases then prevent the rotated dynamics from selecting preferred directions.

Why should that help? Unitary mixing can redistribute amplitudes without revealing information about them. A nonunitary effective map can instead filter components unequally, making outcome records distinguish different inputs. Repeated filtering can purify an initially mixed effective state. The relation between this **dynamical purification** and projected designs is developed by Ippoliti and Ho [@IppolitiHo2023]. Under their nonpurifying conditions, exact design times can coincide. Departing from those conditions allows the time for high moments to exceed ordinary thermalization.

To make the hierarchy precise, choose an error tolerance $\epsilon$ and an equilibrium target. A stable late-time definition is

$$
t_k(\epsilon)=\inf\{t:\Delta_k(t')\leq\epsilon
\text{ for every }t'\geq t\}.
$$ {#eq-pe-design-time}

In a finite isolated system with recurrences, this definition may be inappropriate. One can instead specify a time window, a time-averaged distance, or the fraction of late times satisfying the bound. The convention must be stated before comparing scaling laws. At a fixed time, the moment hierarchy gives $t_{k+1}\geq t_k$ whenever the definition is meaningful with a common tolerance.

A solvable subsystem coupled through a narrow constriction to an infinite random-matrix bath explicitly realizes distinct design times [@IppolitiHo2022]. Its significance is mechanistic: a large bath does not remove a bottleneck through which information about the subsystem must pass. Relaxing a few mean observables can require less information transfer than producing an isotropic distribution of conditional wavefunctions.

The difference can also be understood without a dynamical solution. Suppose an ensemble is supported on many states close to an equatorial circle of a qubit. It may have mean $I/2$ while $\langle Z\rangle_\psi^2$ stays much smaller than the Haar value $1/3$. First-moment relaxation has happened; angular information survives. A proof of ordinary thermalization cannot discard that information because its hypotheses and conclusion never address it.

## A fully specified example: the self-dual kicked Ising chain {#sec-pe-kicked-ising}

We can make the exact-design statement concrete. On an open chain, use Pauli operators $Y_i,Z_i$ and set the time of each Ising segment to one:

$$
\begin{aligned}
U_F&=\exp\!\left(-ih\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i\right)\exp(-iH_Z),\\
H_Z&=J\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}Z_iZ_{i+1}+g\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i
+\frac\pi4(Z_1+Z_N),\qquad J=h=\frac\pi4.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-pe-kicked-ising}

Prepare $|+\rangle^{\otimes N}$, apply $U_F$ an integer $t$ times, retain the first $N_A$ spins, and measure all remaining spins in the $Z$ basis. For $g\notin(\pi/8)\mathbb Z$, the exact result is

$$
\lim_{N_B\to\infty}M_{\mathcal E(t)}^{(k)}
=\frac{P_{\mathrm{sym},A}^{(k)}}{\binom{2^{N_A}+k-1}{k}}
\qquad (t\geq N_A,\ k\text{ fixed}).
$$ {#eq-pe-ising-theorem}

Thus every finite moment reaches its target at the same edge-subsystem time $t_k=N_A$, after taking the bath limit. The boundary fields, preparation, measurement basis, and excluded $g$ values belong to this theorem [@HoChoi2022].

### Why these gates are special

The Ising interaction and the kick are simple matrices, so the special point is accessible without sophisticated tensor notation. With $S=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)$ and $\mathrm{CZ}=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,-1)$,

$$
e^{-i\pi Z\otimes Z/4}=e^{-i\pi/4}(S\otimes S)\mathrm{CZ},
\qquad
e^{-i\pi Y/4}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-pe-ising-elementary}

The first identity follows by checking the four $Z\otimes Z$ eigenvalues; the second follows from $Y^2=I$. The interaction is therefore a controlled phase with local phase rotations, and every matrix element of the kick has magnitude $1/\sqrt2$. In a sum over intermediate spin configurations, amplitudes become equal-magnitude factors with configuration-dependent phases. Combining them into the circuit's tensors gives the self-dual structure: appropriately grouped tensors can be contracted as unitary evolution in the spatial direction as well as in the time direction. The isolated diagonal two-spin interaction is not itself a dual-unitary gate; the grouping matters.

The bath record then selects a sequence of gates on a *dual* chain of $t$ spins. Increasing $N_B$ increases this dual circuit's depth, although physical time stays fixed. Its outcome-counting distribution approaches Haar moments. The remaining boundary contraction maps the $2^t$-dimensional dual state onto the $2^{N_A}$-dimensional physical subsystem. For $t\geq N_A$, cancellations reduce this map to a scalar times a coisometry. A coisometry $Q:\mathbb C^D\to\mathbb C^d$ satisfies $QQ^\dagger=I_d$; it can retain $d$ coordinates after a unitary change of basis. Here $D=2^t$ and $d=2^{N_A}$. The model-specific steps are proving the dual circuit's mixing and this boundary identity. The next calculation explains why those two ingredients imply the claimed ensemble, including its Born weights.

### Deriving the final Haar distribution after projection

Take a Haar vector $u\in\mathbb C^D$ and a fixed coisometry $Q$ with $d$ output dimensions. Write

$$
x=Qu,\qquad R=\|x\|^2,\qquad v=x/\sqrt R.
$$

Choose coordinates with $Q=(I_d\ \ 0)$. Generate $u$ by normalizing independent complex Gaussians. The first $d$ Gaussian components have a direction $v$ independent of their radius; the remaining components do not affect that direction. Consequently $v$ is Haar on $\mathbb C^d$ and is independent of $R$. Also,

$$
\mathbb E R=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[Q\frac{I_D}{D}Q^\dagger\right]=\frac dD.
$$

Now let the physical outcome weight be $w=(D/d)R$. It obeys $\mathbb Ew=1$. Even after this radial Born reweighting,

$$
\mathbb E\!\left[w(|v\rangle\langle v|)^{\otimes k}\right]
=\mathbb Ew\;\mathbb E(|v\rangle\langle v|)^{\otimes k}
=\frac{P_{\mathrm{sym}}^{(k)}}{\binom{d+k-1}{k}}.
$$ {#eq-pe-coisometry-haar}

This is the essential final mechanism. Rotational invariance gives uniform directions; independence of direction and norm ensures that the physical outcome probabilities preserve that uniformity. Replacing the actual Born measure by counting outcomes without this check would leave a gap in the argument. In the kicked Ising construction the scalar multiplying $Q$ supplies precisely the normalization accounted for by $w$.

For $t<N_A$, the dual space has fewer dimensions than the desired output: a map from dimension $2^t$ cannot have row rank $2^{N_A}$. The coisometry mechanism cannot yet apply. More physically, only one boundary feeds entanglement into an edge region, so at most $t$ bits of subsystem entropy can have been produced in this convention, whereas a maximally mixed $N_A$-spin state needs $N_A$ bits. This explains the onset time. A finite bath still has the rank obstruction in @eq-pe-rank-bound; exact equality at every order uses an infinite collection of bath outcomes.

If $A$ lies in the bulk, two boundaries feed entanglement into it. Ordinary thermalization can then occur at $\lceil N_A/2\rceil$, yet higher projected moments need additional time. The topology-dependent rates in @sec-gaussian-nonlocal concern that different geometry [@Shrotriya2025]. The comparison isolates a useful lesson: the number of entanglement cuts can determine first-moment saturation without determining the complete conditional wavefunction distribution.

## Computing a projected moment reproducibly

A small-system calculation should keep normalization and measurement conventions explicit. Reshape a pure-state vector into a matrix $\Psi_{az}$ whose columns correspond to the chosen bath basis. For each column compute $p_z=\sum_a|\Psi_{az}|^2$, normalize the column, construct its $k$-fold projector, and sum with weight $p_z$.

For $k=2$ an alternative avoids tensoring projectors individually: form $v_z=\psi_z\otimes\psi_z$ and accumulate $p_zv_zv_z^\dagger$. The target is $(I+F)/[d_A(d_A+1)]$. Diagonalize the Hermitian difference to obtain the trace norm as the sum of absolute eigenvalues.

Three checks catch common errors. First, $\sum_zp_z=1$ and $\operatorname{Tr}M^{(k)}=1$. Second, partially tracing one replica must recover $M^{(k-1)}$. Third, the computed first moment must equal a direct partial trace of the global state. These are mathematical identities, not assumptions about thermalization.

Postselection on rare outcomes can change the distribution substantially. Likewise, experimental grouping of bath outcomes estimates a coarse-grained ensemble of generally mixed conditional states, rather than the rank-one ensemble defined above. Neither is intrinsically wrong, but the target and interpretation must change with the protocol.

## Exercises and investigations

1. **Unequal Schmidt weights.** For $\sqrt{\lambda}\lvert00\rangle+\sqrt{1-\lambda}\lvert11\rangle$, find the ensembles prepared by $Z$ and $X$ measurements on $B$, their common first moment, and their conditional $Z$ variances. Explain why the $X$-basis states need not be orthogonal. *Hint:* normalize the two vectors $\sqrt{\lambda}\lvert0\rangle\pm\sqrt{1-\lambda}\lvert1\rangle$ and distinguish variance from the second raw moment.

2. **A design witness.** Compute $\mathbb E\langle X\rangle^2$, $\mathbb E\langle Y\rangle^2$, and $\mathbb E\langle Z\rangle^2$ for the uniform ensemble of the six Pauli eigenstates. Determine whether it is a $2$-design and test whether it is a $3$-design. *Hint:* inversion symmetry removes odd powers; a fourth-order test is needed to distinguish this ensemble from the sphere.

3. **Frame-potential calculation.** Evaluate $\mathcal F_2$ for the tetrahedral states in @eq-pe-tetrahedron. *Hint:* for qubits $|\langle\psi_{\boldsymbol n}\vert\psi_{\boldsymbol m}\rangle|^2=(1+\boldsymbol n\cdot\boldsymbol m)/2$; distinct tetrahedral vectors have dot product $-1/3$.

4. **Finite-bath obstruction.** For a two-qubit retained subsystem and an environment of three qubits, determine which design orders are excluded by @eq-pe-rank-bound and give the resulting lower bound on $\Delta_3$. *Hint:* $d_A=4$, $d_B=8$, and $D_3=\binom63$.

5. **Conditional fluctuations of purity.** Split $A=A_1A_2$. Express the ensemble-averaged purity of $\operatorname{Tr}_{A_2}\lvert\psi_z\rangle\langle\psi_z\rvert$ as a trace against $M_{\mathcal E}^{(2)}$. Derive its Haar value. *Hint:* swap only the $A_1$ factors in two copies; use @eq-pe-haar-second.

6. **Numerical experiment in Julia.** Sample a normalized complex Gaussian matrix for several bath sizes at fixed $d_A=2$. Compute $\Delta_1,\Delta_2,\Delta_3$ and repeat over independent matrices. Report means and variation across samples. *Hint:* compare the entire distribution of errors rather than interpreting one favorable sample as a convergence theorem.

7. **A bottleneck question.** Design a local circuit in which a subsystem interacts with the bath only every $m$ layers. Which lower bounds on equilibration follow solely from this schedule? Which additional assumptions would be needed to predict the ratios of design times? *Hint:* distinguish absence of interaction from incomplete scrambling during an interaction.

## Questions at the frontier

There is no single universal formula for all design times. A useful research program asks which physical processes set their hierarchy: entanglement production, transport of conserved quantities, purification of rotated dynamics, or the growth of operator complexity. These processes can coincide in solvable limits and separate in less constrained models.

Another open practical issue is certification. Exact moment tomography becomes expensive because the symmetric space grows as $\binom{d_A+k-1}{k}$. Which experimentally accessible witnesses can establish useful approximate designs without reconstructing that whole operator? A witness can disprove a design by detecting a discrepancy, but agreement with a few witnesses needs additional assumptions to certify closeness.

Finally, the Haar ensemble is appropriate only when no relevant constraint survives. At finite temperature or with a conserved charge, even perfect scrambling cannot erase the constraint. The next chapter develops the corresponding constrained ensembles.
